prompt.context: Our client is a national monthly magazine that wants to restructure its printing division. They currently have 2 facilities where they print their magazines and want to move to only one facility. They hired us to tell them if this is a good idea or not.
prompt.question: Should the client consolidate to one printing facility, and if so, which facility should they keep?

clarifying_info.q: What is the reason behind deciding to restructure the printing division?
clarifying_info.a: The main reason is reduction of costs.

clarifying_info.q: Where are the two facilities located?
clarifying_info.a: One is in Idaho and one is in New Jersey.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current capacity utilization of each facility?
clarifying_info.a: Both facilities can accommodate the total number of magazines they need. They each currently print 50% of the total magazines.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current cost structure?
clarifying_info.a: Total costs = 75 cents/unit; Fixed costs = 35 cents/unit; Total magazines sold per month = 1 million.

clarifying_info.q: What cost savings would consolidation generate?
clarifying_info.a: Moving to one facility would save 20% of the fixed costs.

clarifying_info.q: How would distribution costs change under consolidation?
clarifying_info.a: Keeping New Jersey would increase distribution costs by 2 cents/unit. Keeping Idaho would increase distribution costs by 8 cents/unit.

framework: Understand the objective: cost reduction through consolidation of two printing facilities into one
Analyze current cost structure: break down fixed vs. variable costs per unit
Quantify savings from consolidation: fixed cost reduction from eliminating one facility
Quantify cost increases from consolidation: higher distribution costs depending on which facility is kept
Compare net impact for each facility option (New Jersey vs. Idaho) to determine which yields better economics
Assess risks and non-financial considerations of the move

questions.prompt: What will be the total cost per unit after consolidation, and which facility should the client keep?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate fixed cost savings, then add back the distribution cost increase for each facility option, and compare net savings to determine the preferred location.

math.setup: Fixed cost savings from consolidation: 20% x 35c/unit = 7c/unit. Distribution cost increase: New Jersey +2c/unit; Idaho +8c/unit. Net savings = fixed cost savings minus distribution cost increase.
steps: New Jersey net savings: 7c - 2c = +5c/unit (total cost drops from 75c to 70c/unit)
Idaho net savings: 7c - 8c = -1c/unit (total cost rises from 75c to 76c/unit)
math.answer: Keep New Jersey. It yields a net saving of 5 cents/unit (total cost 70c/unit). Keeping Idaho would increase costs by 1 cent/unit.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks involved in moving to only one printing facility?

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Delivery time increases for customers farther from the single facility
Gas price volatility affecting distribution costs
Single point of failure — any disruption halts all production

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Cost of closing the Idaho facility (severance, lease termination, asset write-downs)
Future increases in sales may exceed single-facility capacity
Cost of materials may change with consolidated purchasing volumes

categories.name: Regulatory & Legal
ideas: Local regulations in New Jersey that could restrict or add costs to operations
Environmental or zoning regulations at the chosen facility

categories.name: Human Capital & Community
ideas: Unemployment impact in Idaho (and potentially New Jersey community relations)
Loss of experienced workforce in the closed facility

recommendation: The client should consolidate to one printing facility and keep the New Jersey location, as it delivers a net cost saving of 5 cents per unit (reducing total cost from 75c to 70c/unit), while closing Idaho would increase costs by 1 cent/unit.
risks: Operational disruption if the single facility faces downtime (no backup)
Distribution cost sensitivity to fuel prices, which could erode savings
Cost of closing the Idaho facility may offset near-term savings
Future volume growth could strain single-facility capacity
Local regulations or labor issues in New Jersey
next_steps: Model the one-time closure costs for Idaho to determine payback period
Assess New Jersey facility capacity headroom against projected sales growth
Develop a transition and change-management plan including workforce impact in Idaho
Review distribution contracts and lock in rates to protect the 2c/unit assumption
